--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Cormack-Jolly-Seber Model' slide-number: true echo: true lang: en --- ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 170%;"}
**Open Populations and the Spatial Cormack-Jolly-Seber Model**
::: {style='font-size: 60%;'} WILD(FISH) 8390
Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
:::
# Overview {visibility="hidden"} ## Open populations
::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} Overview - Population closure is an assumption we make to estimate density in short time periods. - If we want to study the processes governing spatial *and temporal* variation in density, we need to move beyond closed population models. - Open population SCR models allow us to model spatial and temporal variation in survival, recruitment, and movement. ::: ## Types of closure ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Geographic closure - Animals cannot enter or leave the study area - But what is the study area in non-spatial settings? - What is a non-spatial setting? ::: {.fragment} Demographic closure - No births or deaths - Reasonable over short time periods - But temporal dynamics are often of chief interest ::: ::: ## [Two varieties of open mark-recapture models]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Cormack-Jolly-Seber Model - Primarily used to estimate survival - When permanent emigration is possible, estimate is of "apparent survival" ($\phi$) - Apparent survival is the probability of surviving and not leaving the study area permanently - CJS models are not used to estimate abundance or recruitment ::: {.fragment} Jolly-Seber model - Traditionally used to estimate abundance, (apparent) survival, and recruitment ::: ::: {.fragment}
Both classes of models can be made spatially explicit to study movement, among other things
::: ::: # Non-spatial CJS ## Non-spatial CJS model ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Notes ::: {.incremental} - Typical scenario involves "releasing" indviduals and recapturing them over time - We don't model initial capture process - Instead, we "condition on initial capture" - As an example, imagine releasing a bunch of tagged animals in a translocation study - Because we aren't estimating $N$, no data augmentation required - It is possible to estimate parameters using 1 sampling occasion per season - Robust design provides more information about $p$ ::: ::: ## Non-spatial CJS model ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} State model $$ z_{i,t} \sim \mbox{Bernoulli}(z_{i,t-1} \times \phi) $$ ::: {.fragment} Observation model $$ y_{i,t} \sim \mbox{Bernoulli}(z_{i,t} \times p) $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} where - $z_{i,t}$ is "alive state" of individual $i$ at time $t$ - $\phi$ is "apparent survival". Probability of being alive and not permanently emigrating. - $y_{i,t}=1$ if individual was encountered, $y_{i,t}=0$ otherwise. ::: ::: ## [Simulating CJS data without robust design]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Parameters and dimensions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} T <- 10 ## primary periods (eg, years) K <- 1 ## only 1 secondary sampling occasion n <- 25 phi <- 0.7 p <- 0.4 z <- matrix(NA, n, T) y <- matrix(NA, n, T) first <- rpois(n, 1)+1 ## random release dates ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} Generate $z$ and $y$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for(i in 1:n) { z[i,first[i]] <- 1 ## Known alive at release y[i,first[i]] <- 1 for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t-1]*phi) ## Alive/dead state y[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t]*p) ## Data } } ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Simulated CJS data ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} Latent alive/dead state ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} z[,1:7] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [1,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [2,] NA 1 1 1 1 0 0 [3,] NA 1 1 0 0 0 0 [4,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [5,] 1 1 1 0 0 0 0 [6,] NA 1 1 1 1 0 0 [7,] NA NA 1 0 0 0 0 [8,] NA NA NA 1 1 1 1 [9,] 1 1 0 0 0 0 0 [10,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [11,] 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 [12,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [13,] NA NA 1 0 0 0 0 [14,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [15,] NA 1 1 1 1 0 0 [16,] 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 [17,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [18,] 1 1 1 0 0 0 0 [19,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [20,] NA 1 1 0 0 0 0 [21,] NA NA 1 1 0 0 0 [22,] NA 1 1 1 0 0 0 [23,] NA 1 0 0 0 0 0 [24,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [25,] NA 1 1 1 0 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} Encounter histories (data) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y[,1:7] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [1,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [2,] NA 1 0 0 1 0 0 [3,] NA 1 0 0 0 0 0 [4,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [5,] 1 0 1 0 0 0 0 [6,] NA 1 0 0 1 0 0 [7,] NA NA 1 0 0 0 0 [8,] NA NA NA 1 0 0 1 [9,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [10,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [11,] 1 1 0 0 0 0 0 [12,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [13,] NA NA 1 0 0 0 0 [14,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [15,] NA 1 0 0 0 0 0 [16,] 1 0 1 0 1 0 0 [17,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [18,] 1 1 0 0 0 0 0 [19,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [20,] NA 1 0 0 0 0 0 [21,] NA NA 1 1 0 0 0 [22,] NA 1 1 1 0 0 0 [23,] NA 1 0 0 0 0 0 [24,] 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 [25,] NA 1 1 1 0 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Likelihood analysis ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} We can fit CJS models in R with the 'RMark' or 'marked' packages. We'll use 'marked', which requires the capture histories to be formatted as a character vector named `ch`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(marked) y.marked <- ifelse(is.na(y), 0, y) cap.histories <- data.frame( ch=apply(y.marked, 1, paste, collapse="")) head(cap.histories, n=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ch 1 1000000000 2 0100100000 3 0100000000 ``` ::: ::: You can use formulas to model covariate effects. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fm0 <- crm(data=cap.histories, model="CJS", hessian=TRUE, model.parameters=list(Phi=list(formula=~1), p=list(formula=~1))) ``` ::: ::: ## Likelihood analysis Estimates of apparent survival and capture probability. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predict(fm0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $Phi occ estimate se lcl ucl 1 4 0.617999 0.08624809 0.4415182 0.7680138 $p occ estimate se lcl ucl 1 5 0.3242274 0.1095067 0.1526448 0.5609906 ``` ::: ::: ## Non-spatial CJS model in JAGS [CJS-nonspatial.jag](CJS-nonspatial.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { phi ~ dunif(0,1) p ~ dunif(0,1) for(i in 1:n) { z[i,first[i]] <- 1 ## Known alive at time of release for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { z[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t-1]*phi) ## Survives with probability phi y[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t]*p) ## Detected with probability p } } } ``` ::: ::: ## JAGS ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data.nonsp <- list(y=y, n=n, first=first, T=T) ``` ::: Initial values for $z$ matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} zi.nonsp <- matrix(NA, n, T) for(i in 1:n) { zi.nonsp[i,(first[i]+1):T] <- 1 } jags.inits.nonsp <- function() list(phi=runif(1), p=runif(1), z=zi.nonsp) jags.pars.nonsp <- c("phi", "p") ``` ::: Fit the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(jagsUI) jags.post.samples.nonsp <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.nonsp, inits=jags.inits.nonsp, parameters.to.save=jags.pars.nonsp, model.file="CJS-nonspatial.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ::: ## Posterior distributions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(jags.post.samples.nonsp) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/jc1-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: # Spatial CJS ## Spatial CJS Why spatial? - Comes with all the benefits of other SCR models - Allows for movement between primary periods, making it possible to separate survival from permanent emigration - Movement itself may be of interest, such as in studies of dispersal ::: {.fragment} We begin by ignoring movement, but we use the robust design ::: ## [Simulating spatial CJS data with robust design]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} Parameters and data dimensions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} T <- 10 # primary occasions K <- 3 # secondary occasions n <- 25 # nIndividuals phi <- 0.7 p0 <- 0.4 # baseline capture prob sigma <- 0.1 # scale parameter ``` ::: Traps, activity centers, and
detection probability ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} co <- seq(0.25, 0.75, length=5) x <- cbind(rep(co, each=5), rep(co, times=5)) J <- nrow(x) xlim <- ylim <- c(0,1) s <- cbind(runif(n, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(n, ylim[1], ylim[2])) d <- p.sp <- matrix(NA, n, J) for(i in 1:n) { d[i,] <- sqrt((s[i,1]-x[,1])^2 + (s[i,2]-x[,2])^2) p.sp[i,] <- p0*exp(-d[i,]^2/(2*sigma^2)) } ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} Generate $z$ and $y$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- matrix(NA, n, T) y.sp <- array(NA, c(n, J, K, T)) ## 4D array first <- rpois(n, 1)+1 ## random release dates for(i in 1:n) { z[i,first[i]] <- 1 for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t-1]*phi) for(j in 1:J) { y.sp[i,j,1:K,t] <- rbinom(K, 1, z[i,t]*p.sp[i,j]) } } } ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## [Likelihood analysis of spatial CJS model]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} We'll use the R package 'openpopscr'^[Another option is the openCR' package.] for model fitting. It isn't on CRAN, but you can install it from github using the following commands. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(remotes) install_github("r-glennie/openpopscr", build = TRUE, build_opts = c("--no-resave-data", "--no-manual"), build_vignettes = TRUE) library(openpopscr) library(secr) ``` ::: If you're on Windows, you might have to install Rtools first. [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) ::: ## Likelihood analysis of spatial CJS model Begin by making a mask in 'secr' ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} trap.df <- data.frame(x*1000); colnames(trap.df) <- c("x","y") traps <- read.traps(data=trap.df, detector="proximity") mask <- make.mask(traps=traps, buffer=250) plot(mask); points(traps, pch=3, col="blue", lwd=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/mask-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Likelihood analysis of spatial CJS model Format for `secr' ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.sp.secr <- y.sp y.sp.secr[is.na(y.sp)] <- 0 caps <- data.frame(session=1, animal=rep(slice.index(y.sp.secr, 1), y.sp.secr), occasion=rep(slice.index(y.sp.secr, 3:4), y.sp.secr), trap=rep(slice.index(y.sp.secr, 2), y.sp.secr)) capthist <- make.capthist(captures=caps, traps=traps, noccasions=30) ``` ::: Then format for `openpopscr' ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cjs.data <- ScrData$new(capthist, mask, primary=rep(1:10, each=3)) ``` ::: ## Likelihood analysis Create the model object and then fit it ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod <- CjsModel$new(list(lambda0~1, sigma~1, phi~1), cjs.data, start=list(lambda0=1.5, sigma=50, phi=0.5)) mod$fit() mod ``` ::: Back-transform ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod$get_par("lambda0", k = 1, j = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3824823 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mod$get_par("sigma", k = 1, j = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 102.0998 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mod$get_par("phi", k = 1, m=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5708015 ``` ::: ::: ## Spatial CJS model in JAGS [CJS-spatial.jag](CJS-spatial.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { phi ~ dunif(0,1) ## Apparent survival p0 ~ dunif(0,1) ## Baseline capture prob sigma ~ dunif(0, 2) ## Scale parameter of detection function for(i in 1:n) { ## Loop over individuals s[i,1] ~ dunif(xlim[1], xlim[2]) # static activity centers s[i,2] ~ dunif(ylim[1], ylim[2]) for(j in 1:J) { ## Loop over traps d[i,j] <- sqrt((s[i,1] - x[j,1])^2 + (s[i,2] - x[j,2])^2) p[i,j] <- p0*exp(-d[i,j]^2/(2*sigma^2)) ## Capture prob } z[i,first[i]] <- 1 ## Condition on first encounter for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { z[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t-1]*phi) ## Model subsequent encounters for(j in 1:J) { for(k in 1:K) { y[i,j,k,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t]*p[i,j]) } } } } } ``` ::: ::: ## JAGS Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data.sp <- list(y=y.sp, n=n, first=first, x=x, J=J, K=K, T=T, xlim=xlim, ylim=ylim) ``` ::: Initial values for $z$ matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} zi.sp <- matrix(NA, n, T) for(i in 1:n) { zi.sp[i,(first[i]+1):T] <- 1 } jags.inits.sp <- function() list(phi=runif(1), z=zi.sp) jags.pars.sp <- c("phi", "p0", "sigma") ``` ::: Fit the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.post.samples.sp <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.sp, inits=jags.inits.sp, parameters.to.save=jags.pars.sp, model.file="CJS-spatial.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ## Posterior distributions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(jags.post.samples.sp) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/jc2-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: # Spatial CJS with movement ## Modeling dispersal among years What if activity centers move between years? - Could affect estimates of detection parameters - More importantly, might provide opportunity to study dispersal Potential movement models} - Random walk: ${\bm s}_t \sim \mbox{Normal}({\bm s}_{t-1}, \tau^2)$ - Random walk with attraction point: ${\bm s}_t \sim \mbox{Normal}({\bm s}_{t-1} + \rho(\bar{\bm s} - {\bm s}_{t-1}), \tau^2)$ - Extensions can be made to allow for resource selection, landscape resistance, etc.^[https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.3473]. ## Simulating spatial CJS data with dispersal ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} Parameters and data dimensions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} T <- 10; K <- 5; n <- 25 ## same as before phi <- 0.9; p0 <- 0.4; sigma <- 0.05 ## dispersal parameter (of random walk) tau <- 0.05 ``` ::: Activity centers take a random walk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## state-space should be bigger xlim <- ylim <- c(0, 1) first <- rpois(n, 1)+1 s <- array(NA, c(n, 2, T)) for(i in 1:n) { s[i,,first[i]] <- cbind(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2])) for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { s[i,1,t] <- rnorm(1, s[i,1,t-1], tau) s[i,2,t] <- rnorm(1, s[i,2,t-1], tau) } } d <- p <- array(NA, c(n, J, T)) for(i in 1:n) { for(t in 1:T) { d[i,,t] <- sqrt((s[i,1,t]-x[,1])^2 + (s[i,2,t]-x[,2])^2) p[i,,t] <- p0*exp(-d[i,,t]^2 / (2*sigma^2)) } } ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} Generate $z$ and $y$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- matrix(NA, n, T) y.move <- array(NA, c(n, J, T)) for(i in 1:n) { z[i,first[i]] <- 1 for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t-1]*phi) for(j in 1:J) { y.move[i,j,t] <- rbinom(1, K, z[i,t]*p[i,j,t]) } } } ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Movement of activity center 1 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(t(s[1,,]), pch=16, type="o", xlab="x", ylab="y", xlim=c(0, 1), ylim=c(0, 1), asp=1, col="blue") points(x, pch=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/s1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ## Movement of all activity centers ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/s-all-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ## Spatial CJS model with dispersal in JAGS [CJS-spatial-move.jag](CJS-spatial-move.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { phi ~ dunif(0,1) p0 ~ dunif(0,1) sigma ~ dunif(0, 2) tau ~ dunif(0, 2) tauprec <- 1/tau^2 # must convert tau to precision for(i in 1:n) { s[i,1,first[i]] ~ dunif(xlim[1], xlim[2]) s[i,2,first[i]] ~ dunif(ylim[1], ylim[2]) for(j in 1:J) { d[i,j,first[i]] <- sqrt((s[i,1,first[i]] - x[j,1])^2 + (s[i,2,first[i]] - x[j,2])^2) p[i,j,first[i]] <- p0*exp(-d[i,j,first[i]]^2/(2*sigma^2)) } z[i,first[i]] <- 1 for(t in (first[i]+1):T) { s[i,1,t] ~ dnorm(s[i,1,t-1], tauprec)#T(xlim[1], xlim[2]) s[i,2,t] ~ dnorm(s[i,2,t-1], tauprec)#T(ylim[1], ylim[2]) for(j in 1:J) { d[i,j,t] <- sqrt((s[i,1,t] - x[j,1])^2 + (s[i,2,t] - x[j,2])^2) p[i,j,t] <- p0*exp(-d[i,j,t]^2/(2*sigma^2)) } z[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t-1]*phi) for(j in 1:J) { y[i,j,t] ~ dbin(z[i,t]*p[i,j,t], K) # for(k in 1:K) { y[i,j,k,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t]*p[i,j,t]) } } } } } ``` ::: ::: ## JAGS Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jd.sp.move <- list(y=y.move, n=n, first=first, x=x, J=J, K=K, T=T, xlim=xlim, ylim=ylim) ``` ::: Initial values for $z$, and parameters to monitor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} zi <- matrix(NA, n, T) for(i in 1:n) { zi[i,(first[i]+1):T] <- 1 } ji.sp.move <- function() list(phi=runif(1), z=zi, s=s) ## Cheating with s jp.sp.move <- c("phi", "p0", "sigma", "tau") good1 <- which.max(rowSums(z, na.rm=TRUE)+rowSums(y.move, na.rm=TRUE)) time1 <- first[good1]:T jp.s1x <- paste0("s[", good1, ",1,", time1, "]") jp.s1y <- paste0("s[", good1, ",2,", time1, "]") jp.z1 <- paste0("z[", good1, ",", time1, "]") ``` ::: Fit the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jps.sp.move <- jags.basic(data=jd.sp.move, inits=ji.sp.move, parameters.to.save= c(jp.sp.move, jp.s1x, jp.s1y, jp.z1), model.file="CJS-spatial-move.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ## Posterior distributions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(jps.sp.move[,jp.sp.move]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/jc3-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Posterior movement path ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-CJS_files/figure-revealjs/jc3-s-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Summary Spatial CJS models allow for inference about survival, movement, and capture probability. We could have considered many other movement models. Next, we'll use Jolly-Seber models to study spatio-temporal variation in abundance and recruitment.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
